risks.summary: An advisory attached to a settled request reads as the opinion behind the decision.
risks.detail: NEX-036 found that RecommendApprovalDecision built an advisory for any approval the caller owned, including ones already approved, denied or revoked, while its docstring and the route summary described advice about a *pending* approval. A score attached to a settled request invites a reviewer to read it as the opinion that produced the decision, and a later reader to read it as one that informed it - in an audit trail that is exactly the wrong inference. It also spent provider time and a withholding count on a question nobody could act on. Fixed: the use case now refuses with 409 when the request is not pending, or when its bound has passed under the use case's own clock (never the wall clock - see R29). Pinned by four mutation-checked tests plus one asserting the live case still works.
risks.status: closed by NEX-036 - CI green at 90eea0c, polled 2026-11-25T18:45Z (Backend id 139429822539, Frontend id 139429823232)

risks.summary: Withholding is counted per process but nothing exports the count.
risks.detail: NEX-033 introduced the WithholdingRecorder port and NEX-032 made each advisory report which fields were withheld and why. Both are per-response or per-process observations. An operator cannot currently answer 'how often are advisories thinner than they should be' without reading individual responses, so a systematic over-cap withholding would be visible in aggregate nowhere. This is a monitoring gap, not a correctness gap: the security invariant (withhold rather than leak) holds. Carried forward as NEX-037. CLOSED (NEX-037): GET /api/v1/ops/withholding-report returns advisories_total, over_cap_advisories_total, over_cap_fields_total and over_cap_rate, so the rate R34 asked for is now a number an operator can alert on. The aggregate spans every tenant, so it is gated on OPS_OPERATOR_USER_IDS - empty by default, and empty means nobody, not everybody. A non-operator receives 404 rather than 403 so probing cannot confirm the endpoint exists. The response carries counts only: no field name, value, note id or user id. Malformed operator ids fail at startup rather than matching nobody silently.
risks.status: closed by NEX-037 - 4/4 completed/success at 5c0575b, every head_sha equal to that SHA, polled 2026-11-25T18:57Z.

risks.summary: A bounded context contract has now met real note text; the hand-assembled-declassification gap is closed by type.
risks.detail: NEX-028 caps a context field's value at 200 characters and an envelope at 32 fields, and names fields with stable lowercase identifiers. Every current caller is a test, so none of those bounds has met real note text or a real note title. The first production caller (tool-gateway classification or the approval-recommendation path) is the first genuine test; if a bound is too tight, widening it is a contract change requiring review, not a tweak to a constant. Related honest gap, documented on DecisionRequest.from_context: context_hash is a plain str, so a caller can hand-assemble one, which means taking the declassification decision personally. A later slice can narrow the field to a type only an envelope can construct. UPDATE (NEX-029): ContextEnvelope now has a production caller - the advisory route builds one from a real stored approval record, so the 32-field and 200-char bounds have met real approval data. They have still not met real note text, and context_hash is still a plain str. CLOSED (NEX-030): context_hash is now ContextHash, constructible only through ContextHash._mint, which only ContextEnvelope calls. A caller-assembled string is rejected by decisioning._validate_context_hash. The bounds (32 fields, 200 chars) have still not met real note text - that remains a live observation, not a code gap. CLOSED (NEX-031): the bounds have now met a real stored note body at MAX_CONTENT_BYTES (64 KiB, ~300x the 200-char field cap) and an over-cap record-derived value is withheld rather than raising, so a legal note can no longer deny the advisory. The note-text observation is closed; the stated str.__new__ residual on ContextHash is unchanged and deliberate.
risks.status: closed (NEX-030 + NEX-031)

risks.summary: The decision contract's bounds had only ever met a stub; a conformance suite now exercises each against a hostile payload, and building it found four real defects.
risks.detail: NEX-027 caps a decision's rationale at 400 characters, its confidence/score at [0.0, 1.0], and its choice set at the caller's candidates. The stub adapter always answers cheaply, so no bound had met a payload that tested it. NEX-035 ships tests/agent/test_decision_provider_conformance.py: assert_provider_conformance is the contract a real vendor adapter is run through, with meta-tests proving the suite rejects a hostile fake one violation at a time. Building it exposed a blind spot the bounds never covered - the provider's own NAME. EvaluateDecision guarded everything a provider answered and nothing about what it called itself, though a name is third-party input that lands in audit records, log fields and API responses. Fixed: validate_provider_name enforces the declared 80-char bound plus an identifier shape (a newline in a name is a log-injection vector); _safe_provider_name reads the name once, before anything else can fail, and degrades to 'unidentified' on a raise or a non-identifier, so third-party code cannot break a caller that has a deterministic fallback; and a ValidationError raised through decide is classified MALFORMED_OUTPUT rather than PROVIDER_ERROR, so an operator is not sent to check connectivity when the payload is the problem. Residual: the suite proves a CONFORMING adapter behaves. It cannot prove a vendor's model produces good judgments - that is an evaluation question, not a contract one.
risks.status: closed (NEX-035, 4/4 completed/success at 12f6fa9, polled 2026-11-25T18:14Z)

risks.summary: A validity bound written by one clock and read by another gives the wrong answer in both directions.
risks.detail: NEX-026: ApprovalRequest.open stamped expires_at from the caller's Clock port, but the decision path called is_expired, which reads the module wall clock. A request opened on a clock behind the wall clock was judged already lapsed, so a human could not decide a live request; a request opened on a clock ahead of the wall clock was judged still valid after its bound passed, so consent outlived the bound it was granted under. Every existing expiry test used one clock for both open and decide, so the two readings always agreed and the defect was structurally invisible. The repository adapter was already correct, which is why no integration test caught it either. General rule: for every bound, name the clock that writes it and assert the reader uses the same one - and test the disagreement, not just the happy path, because a single-clock suite cannot see this class at all.
risks.status: closed by NEX-026, VERIFIED at b46e2e3

risks.summary: A grant can outlive the consent that justified it, because the grant does not name the consent.
risks.detail: An approval records agent_id and no delegation, so it cannot be attributed to a surviving delegation when one is withdrawn - and nothing withdrew it. RevokeDelegation revoked the delegation and its tokens but left the agent operational, so after re-delegation a token from the new delegation could spend an approval granted under the withdrawn one. RevokeAgent left approvals approved too: latent while the agent check blocks use, but any reactivation path would inherit pre-emergency-stop grants. Closed by NEX-025 on both paths. General rule: for every piece of live authority, ask what revokes it and follow the chain to the end - revoking the container is not enough if the authority is keyed to something that survives it. Same shape as R23 and R26.
risks.status: closed on both revocation paths by NEX-025 (d481bd0), 4/4 completed/success observed 2026-11-25T13:18Z

risks.summary: A terminal state in one record is not a terminal state in the record that describes the same event.
risks.detail: NEX-023 closed this on the resolve path: InvokeTool commits its ToolInvocation as `started` before entering the handler (correct - a crash must leave a trace), and ResolveInterruptedStep had settled the run without closing that row. NEX-024 found the same defect on the other settle path: AbortAgentRun flipped the run to aborted and never sealed the link, while AgentRun.abort also left a `started` step inside a terminal run. Both halves now settle, in one transaction. General rule, now proven to recur once: any operation that makes a run terminal must settle its mid-flight steps AND seal their invocations in the same transaction. A third settle path reopens this. Two records that disagree are not a partial success.
risks.status: closed on both existing settle paths (resolve: NEX-023; abort: NEX-024)

risks.summary: A field can be persisted, foreign-keyed, and written on every create — and still never be read by the check that needs it.
risks.detail: NEX-022: agent_runs.delegation_id was written by PlanAgentRun on every plan, carried a FK to agent_delegations, and was never consulted by AdvanceAgentRun._load_for_agent, which compared only agent_id. So a token from a different delegation could drive a run, and revoking the planning delegation did not stop it. The schema asserted the binding mattered; the read path disagreed, and nothing failed. General rule: for every security-relevant column, grep for the reads, not just the writes. A column written and never read is either dead or a missing check — decide which, in writing.
risks.status: open - standing environment hazard; the rule is to avoid heredocs entirely

risks.summary: A control enforced on every path someone thought of can still miss a path that establishes the same identity.
risks.detail: NEX-006 closed the offboarding gap by calling ensure_tenant_access on the three human identity paths (OIDC callback, session resolution, bearer provider). Agent-token resolution was a fourth way to establish an identity and never called it, so a suspended delegator's agent stayed fully operational for as long as its token lived. The gap survived because the shared seam looked complete: every caller of ensure_tenant_access was correct, and nothing enumerated the callers that were missing. Lesson: when a check is 'the one place', list every identity-establishing path and assert each one calls it, rather than trusting the seam's existence. Closed for agent tokens by 990557d.
risks.status: open - standing environment hazard; the rule is to avoid heredocs entirely

risks.summary: A governance gate can be structurally unusable while every test stays green.
risks.detail: NEX-016: human approval was implemented end to end (requests, decisions, expiry, revocation, HTTP routes, 8 tests) yet a durable run could never honour an approval. Two independent defects each alone made resumption impossible: the run failed terminally on the pause, and the unique (agent_id, idempotency_key) constraint was permanently consumed by the denial record. No test covered 'approve, then continue', so the suite was green through a decorative control. The general lesson: a security control needs a test of the full decision-to-effect path, not tests of each half.

risks.title: Coordinator CI notes go stale silently and read as current forever
risks.detail: Three claims in this repo's own docs were false at run start. STATE.md called ca15eb1 'docs-only and unclaimed' when it was 4/4 completed/success at that exact SHA. STATE.md carried PR counters of 28,385 additions / 88 commits when the PR object said 28,409 / 89. BACKLOG.md said 'CI has not yet run on c18bac7' when c18bac7 was 4/4 green. Each was written once at push time and never revisited. A note phrased 'CI has not yet run on X' has no expiry and is indistinguishable, to a later reader, from 'CI failed on X'. Mitigation: name the poll timestamp in any such note, and re-poll any not-yet-observed claim in the next run where that commit is reachable. Polling costs seconds. UPDATE (NEX-2026-11-25-35): a fourth instance was caught by reconciliation rather than by a reader - CHECKPOINT.json recorded NEX-033 as 'pytest 877 passed' when the true baseline at bf84a7c was 873; 877 was the count after NEX-034's tests were added. Corrected in task_statuses.NEX-033. Also caught: next_action named NEX-034 for work NEX-033 had already shipped, which would have re-implemented a delivered feature. Both were stale intent fields, not stale CI notes, so the class is broader than CI: any field recording 'what to do next' or 'what the numbers were' decays the same way.
risks.status: mitigated - one instance caught this run

risks.summary: A verifier that only checks a seal when the seal exists can be defeated by deleting the seal.
risks.detail: NEX-012 sealed each invocation's verdict in outcome_hash and NEX-012's tests proved that editing the verdict without touching the seal is caught. But verify_chain recomputed the seal only when one was present, so nulling outcome_hash and completed_at together removed the evidence instead of contradicting it, and the chain verified clean. The test attacked the weaker forgery. General rule: for every field a check reads, ask what the check does when that field is absent, and treat absence as a break wherever the state machine says the field must be present. Closed by NEX-018.
risks.status: open - standing environment hazard; the rule is to avoid heredocs entirely

risks.summary: Withholding is now observable per field; the remaining gap is that nothing aggregates it over time.
risks.detail: NEX-031 made an over-cap record-derived value withheld rather than fatal, which is the right failure direction. NEX-032 closes the blind spot that created: every recommendation now reports which fields were withheld and why, so a thinner-than-expected advisory is visible rather than inferred. What remains is aggregation - no metric counts how often an over-cap withholding happens across advisories. If a real note field routinely exceeds MAX_FIELD_VALUE_LENGTH, the per-recommendation record will show it but nothing will alert on it. That is a monitoring task, not a correctness gap; the security invariant holds.
risks.status: closed by NEX-032 (per-field observability); aggregation is a separate follow-up

risks.summary: The redactor's vocabulary is finite; the structural hole is closed, the word list is not.
risks.detail: NEX-034 replaced an eleven-string exact-match denylist with word-based shape matching, so a credential spelled differently (client_secret vs clientSecret vs CLIENT-SECRET) now reaches one verdict, and a new vendor's spelling is caught without editing a set. What remains is vocabulary: a credential named with a word on neither _SENSITIVE_WORDS nor _SENSITIVE_WORD_PAIRS would still pass. This is a strictly better failure mode than the predecessor - widening vocabulary is additive and cheap, whereas the old matcher required one entry per spelling. Do not treat this as closed; if a real credential name is found to leak, add the word AND a test naming that exact spelling.
risks.status: open - accepted residual, documented

risks.summary: The ops allowlist is a per-user grant with no rotation story and no audit trail of who read the aggregate.
detail: NEX-037 gates /api/v1/ops/withholding-report on OPS_OPERATOR_USER_IDS and refuses everyone else with 404. That is the right default-deny shape, but the grant is a static environment variable: there is no way to see who currently holds it from inside the system, no expiry, and no record of which operator read the totals and when. The response is counts-only, so the disclosure is small, but an operator allowlist that cannot be audited is a governance gap rather than a security hole. The wider fix is the same one the platform already needs for every privileged read - a scoped capability grant with an audit record - so this should be folded into that slice rather than solved ad hoc here. Until then, changing the variable requires a redeploy, which at least makes each change a reviewable event.
risks.status: open - accepted residual, to be folded into the scoped-capability work

risks.summary: The HTTP adapter's response size bound is enforced after the body is read, so it bounds what is parsed, not what is held in memory.
detail: HttpDecisionProvider checks len(response.content) > 64 KiB only after httpx has already materialised the whole response. A hostile or badly broken configured vendor can therefore make the process hold an arbitrarily large body in memory before the adapter refuses to parse it.

This is judged acceptable for now and recorded rather than silently accepted, because the threat model is a buggy or compromised *configured* vendor, not an attacker who chooses the URL: the endpoint comes from operator configuration and must be https. A streaming read with a running byte budget is the fix when that threat model widens.
The module docstring states the limit explicitly, so a future reader is not misled by the presence of a 64 KiB constant into believing memory is bounded.
risks.status: CLOSED - run NEX-2026-11-27-44
risks.closure_evidence: The adapter now opens the response with httpx.stream and enforces the 64 KiB cap while reading: a declared oversized Content-Length returns MALFORMED_OUTPUT before any body byte is read, an unannounced body is abandoned the instant the running total passes the cap (leaving the context manager closes the stream rather than draining it), and a non-200 body is never read at all. Three tests fail against the previous implementation and they assert on chunk counts / a body that raises if read, so a drain would fail them. The residual limit - the cap bounds size, not duration - stays recorded in the module docstring as an open, honest limit.
